explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The text says Jehoahaz "did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his fathers had done." His father Josiah turned to the LORD with all his heart (2 Kings 23:25), but the text doesn't say Jehoahaz followed that road. Three months on the throne, and that's the record we get.

That's right. The text says Jehoahaz "did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his fathers had done." His father Josiah was a king who turned to the LORD with all his heart (2 Kings 23:25), so this son stepping off that road stands out. A short reign, and the verdict is already written.

explanations.answer: So he can't reign in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Yes, the text gives the reason plainly. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, imprisoned Jehoahaz at Riblah "so that he could not reign in Jerusalem." Neco wanted that throne empty. Nobody had to guess his motive, because the verse hands it over.

explanations.answer: So he can serve in Egypt's army
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but the text never mentions an army. It says Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, locked Jehoahaz up at Riblah "so that he could not reign in Jerusalem." The whole point was keeping him off the throne. No uniform, no drills, just a locked door.

explanations.answer: So he can learn Egypt's ways
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have any lessons going on here. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, imprisoned Jehoahaz at Riblah "so that he could not reign in Jerusalem." That's the reason the verse gives. This was a lockup, not a training program.

That's the one. The text says Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, "made Eliakim son of Josiah king in place of his father Josiah." Eliakim was another son of Josiah, so he came from the royal family. Still, the pick came from Egypt. Judah didn't get a vote.

Not here. Earlier, the people of the land made Jehoahaz king (2 Kings 23:30), so you might expect Judah to pick again. But this time the text says Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, made Eliakim king. The elders aren't even in this verse.

The priests don't show up in this part of the story. The text says Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, "made Eliakim son of Josiah king in place of his father Josiah." The choice came from the one holding Jehoahaz in prison. Nobody in Jerusalem got to hand out the crown.
Correct. The text says Neco "took Jehoahaz and carried him off to Egypt." Pharaoh Neco was Egypt's king, so he took his prisoner home with him. Jehoahaz went from Judah's throne to a foreign land.

explanations.answer: Lets him go back to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That would be a gentler ending, but the text doesn't give it. Jerusalem now had a new king, Jehoiakim, and Neco took Jehoahaz and carried him off to Egypt. No homecoming for him. I think that's a heavy turn for a man who'd only been king three months.

Hamath is the land where Riblah sits, which is why it's in the story. But the text doesn't give Jehoahaz any job there. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, took him and carried him off to Egypt. Governor is a nice title, and he never got it.
Yes. The text says Neco carried Jehoahaz off to Egypt, "where he died." He was twenty-three when he became king, and he never returned to Jerusalem. It's a sad ending, and the text states it plainly.

The text actually says it the other way. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, carried Jehoahaz off to Egypt, "where he died." He didn't make it back to Judah. I think this is one of the heavier lines in the passage.

That's it. Jehoiakim taxed the land and took the silver and gold from the people, "each according to his wealth." So the amount depended on what each person had. Pharaoh Neco sent the bill, and the people of Judah got handed the payment.

Age is a good guess, but the text doesn't use it. Jehoiakim took the silver and gold from the people "each according to his wealth." How much you owed depended on what you had, not how many birthdays you'd counted. The bill for Pharaoh Neco, Egypt's king, landed on everybody.

Tribe is a sensible guess, but the text doesn't say it. Jehoiakim taxed the land and took the silver and gold from the people "each according to his wealth." The amount followed what a person owned. Pharaoh Neco was Egypt's king, and he wanted his payment however it got collected.

Right. The text says Jehoiakim "became his vassal for three years." A vassal is a king who answers to a stronger king. So the man Pharaoh Neco had put on the throne ended up under Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Judah's king kept changing bosses.

The text doesn't send him there. Egypt's Pharaoh Neco was the one who made Jehoiakim king, so it might seem natural. But when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, invaded, the text says Jehoiakim "became his vassal for three years." He stayed and served.

Hiding makes sense on a scary day, but the text doesn't mention it. When Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, invaded, Jehoiakim "became his vassal for three years." He served the invader instead of ducking him. No hiding spot is listed.
Yes. The text says he served for three years "until he turned and rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar." Nebuchadnezzar was the king of Babylon. So Jehoiakim went from serving him to turning against him.

The text says the opposite. Jehoiakim was Nebuchadnezzar's vassal for three years, "until he turned and rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar." Nebuchadnezzar was the king of Babylon. The serving stopped when the rebelling started.

That's right. The text says, "the LORD sent Chaldean, Aramean, Moabite, and Ammonite raiders against Jehoiakim in order to destroy Judah." It happened "according to the word that the LORD had spoken through His servants the prophets." These raiders came because the LORD sent them.

Pharaoh Neco, Egypt's king, did put Jehoiakim on the throne, so it's an understandable guess. But the text says it plainly: "the LORD sent" these raiders. Neco isn't part of this verse. This time the sender is named, and it's the LORD.

Assyria isn't in this part of the story. The text says "the LORD sent Chaldean, Aramean, Moabite, and Ammonite raiders against Jehoiakim." That's the answer the verse gives. No Assyrian king gets credit here.

That's not what the text says. It says Manasseh "had filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD was unwilling to forgive." Manasseh was an earlier king of Judah (2 Kings 21:1). I think this is a heavy part of the passage, and the text doesn't soften it.

Correct. The text says Manasseh "had filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD was unwilling to forgive." Manasseh was an earlier king of Judah (2 Kings 21:1). This is a heavy part of the story, and the text says it straight.

Yes. The text says Jehoiakim "rested with his fathers, and his son Jehoiachin reigned in his place." The throne went from father to son. That's a different pattern from the first half of the passage, where Pharaoh Neco did the choosing.

Gedaliah comes up later in the book as a governor, not a king (2 Kings 25:22). Here the text says that when Jehoiakim "rested with his fathers, his son Jehoiachin reigned in his place." The crown stayed in the family this time.

Shaphan was a scribe in Josiah's day (2 Kings 22:3), and scribes keep records, not crowns. In this passage the text says Jehoiakim "rested with his fathers, and his son Jehoiachin reigned in his place." The king's own son took over. The scribe stayed at his desk.

explanations.answer: Babylon had taken all his territory
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The king of Egypt stayed home "because the king of Babylon had taken all his territory, from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River." That's a big stretch of land. Nebuchadnezzar's reach was now much bigger.

explanations.answer: He had made peace with Judah
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention any peace deal. It says the king of Egypt stayed in his land "because the king of Babylon had taken all his territory, from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River." The reason was Babylon, not a handshake with Judah.

explanations.answer: A plague had struck his army
explanations.explanation: No plague is mentioned in this passage. The text gives the reason: "the king of Babylon had taken all his territory, from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River." He didn't march out again because Babylon held his land. Nothing in the verse mentions his army getting sick.
